Organization That Recently Apologized To Galileo
Blames Marijuana For Shooting By Man With Brain Cyst

Closing the books on the first killings within Vatican precincts in 150 years, the officials said a nine-month probe into the incident led investigators to the same conclusion they expressed at the time: That Cedric Tornay, 23, shot Col. Alois Estermann and his wife, Gladys, in their Vatican apartment with his service revolver before killing himself—dismissing the possibility of other suspects and ruling out a conspiracy.

But for the first time, the Vatican disclosed evidence that Tornay was a marijuana smoker and said it could not rule out that he was a chronic drug user, which "would further explain his behavior." It also said an autopsy revealed a cyst the size of a pigeon’s egg in Tornay’s brain.

Nothing in the 10-page report materially altered the Vatican’s initial explanation of the May 4 slayings: That the guardsman was driven by hatred of the newly appointed commander and that he carried out the killings in a fit of anger over Estermann’s refusal to give him a medal.

A report in a Swiss newspaper Sunday quoted Tornay’s mother as claiming that all three were victims of a plot and that her son was wrongly accused "in the attempt to hide a probably unconfessable truth."

Vatican spokesman Joaquin Navarro-Valls said he understood the mother’s grief but that "the results of the investigation are what they are, and the reality can’t be canceled."

The Swiss Guard, the pope’s picturesquely attired personal security force, was founded in 1506 and draws volunteer recruits from among young Swiss Catholic men, generally army veterans.

(Marijuananews note: An organization that wishes its statements on public affairs to be taken seriously should take more seriously its own obligations to the truth. It would seem that having suffered the embarrassment of having to apologize to Galileo five hundred years after the fact might have taught them something. Apparently not. Consider the following points of moral concern:
1. A man commits a double murder and then suicide, either as the result of an organic brain disease or the result of using a drug. If it was the former, he is not morally responsible for his actions and his immortal soul may not be held accountable for his actions. If his actions were the result of the irresponsible use of a substance that is known to cause homicidal delusions, then he is morally responsible for his actions. So it is of relevance that marijuana -- unlike alcohol -- is not commonly associated with acts of violence. This fact is readily ascertainable and very relevant to this event. The condition of souls is of some concern to the Vatican, I understand. Although perhaps even there reefer madness takes precedence, as it does on the religious right in DEAland.
2. The Vatican is guilty of violating the 9th Commandment, giving false evidence against this man, by implying that these terrible acts may have been the result of a voluntary act when there is a perfectly good medical explanation for this.
3. The mother of the accused is grieving for her son, and the word that he had an organic brain disorder would be of great comfort to her, as well as to the survivors of the two people he is accused of killing.
4. This statement will be used to justify the use of violence against marijuana users, especially in some Catholic countries. Hence it is a violation of the 9th Commandment, giving false evidence against marijuana users.
5. The Vatican is yet to speak out against the persecution of the sick and dying who use medical marijuana.
6. This statement by the Vatican is obviously not ex cathedra and is not subject to the doctrine of Papal Infallibility, rather is an arrogant display of invincible ignorance by a functionary who has embarrassed the Holy See and the faithful.
7. I trust that we will not have to wait 500 years for The Church to apologize for this.
8. This is not a matter that should concern only Roman Catholics, but anyone who takes religion seriously.)
